name: Aaron Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior on the performance marketing side at a sports drink brand. That means paid ads on social media and search: I set up the ads, test different versions, and report every morning on what sold. I use AI every single day, it writes me forty ad variations before my coffee's cold. The part I'm still bad at is judgement, like where to put the budget, and my lead Femi catches my mistakes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's numbers, you know straight away if something worked. What gets to me is being on lower pay with a student loan, and only having about two weeks of money saved. I share a flat with my cousin to keep rent down. There's this brand and maybe two agencies in our city, that's it for jobs like mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI's a good tool, not magic, which is pretty much what I already say. I'd post a little before-and-after of how much faster ad testing is. People at the gym would roll their eyes at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine with this one. My job stays, I keep my speed advantage, and the brand carries on. The money's still the tight bit, the student loan comes out every month whatever AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools hard and try to get the budget judgement right, so Femi trusts me with a bigger slice. I'd pick up a couple of freelance ad setups for local gyms on weekends. And I'd try to get to one month saved by summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit restless, because I want more money than I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could a gym pay you for ad setups?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a hundred a month each to run their local ads. Two gyms would cover my phone and my share of the electric. Not life changing, but it's a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're bad at budget judgement. How does that feel when the numbers come in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad, honestly. Last month I spent too much on a video that flopped, and Femi had to explain it upstairs. The tools don't save you from that kind of mistake yet.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool, not magic**, which I already say.
I'd post a **before-and-after** of faster ad testing.
think: I think my **job stays** and I keep my speed edge.
The **student loan** still makes money tight.
do: Improve my **budget judgement** so Femi trusts me more.
Run **freelance ads** for two local gyms at weekends.
S0.quote: The student loan comes out every month whatever AI does.
fieldNote: He's **confident** in this picture but restless about low pay.
His weak spot is **budget judgement**, not speed.
He starts a small **side income** even when nothing changes.

steps.text: Use AI tools daily to test more ad versions
Run local ads for two gyms for about a hundred a month each
Save one month of expenses by summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to learn the tools, not fight them. At work I'd offer to train others. Online I'd be the guy sharing tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, buying ads is literally on that card's list. The tools would set up and test ads by themselves. One senior person with the AI tools could run what three junior ad buyers do now. I'm fast with the tools, but so will everyone be, and I'm still the junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Femi to let me own the automated ad system for one product line, so I'm running the machine. I'd grow the gym side gig to four or five clients. And I'd start learning the data side properly, maybe a short course in analytics, because that's harder to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit wired. It's like a race I could win, but I'm starting from the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the brand cut the team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time on the freelance thing for a while and look at agencies in other cities. My cousin would cover rent for a month if I asked. I wouldn't want to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your cousin about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've got a plan and two backup plans. He'd laugh, because I always say that. But this time I'd mean it.

I'd offer to **train colleagues** and share tips online.
think: I think **buying ads** is right there on the card.
One senior could run **three juniors' work** with the tools.
do: Ask Femi to let me own the **automated ad system** for one product line.
Grow the gym side gig to **four or five clients**.
feel: Anxious and **wired**, like a race I'm starting **from the back**.
S1.quote: One senior person with the AI tools could run what three junior ad buyers do now.
fieldNote: He wants to **run the machine** rather than compete with it.
He sees **analytics** as harder to automate than ad copy.
His cousin is a quiet **safety net** he'd rather not use.

steps.text: Ask to run the automated ad system for one drink range
Grow gym ad clients to four or five
Take a short online course in marketing analytics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need to move fast, and the government needs some kind of bridge for people. I'd be practical about it, not angry. I'd still be posting tips, but they'd feel a bit pointless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years is nothing. If AI does any thinking work better and cheaper, my whole job is gone, and my side gig too, because gyms can just use the AI themselves. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me, I don't do anything with my hands at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast towards something physical and with people. I played football to a decent level, so I'd do a coaching qualification and get on at a gym as a personal trainer. I'd keep doing ads until the last day and save every bit I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be moving, but it's the kind of moving you do when the building's on fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Personal trainers face robots around 2031 too. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But I think people pay a trainer to shout at them and care whether they turn up. A robot can count reps, but it can't make you feel guilty for skipping the gym.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, then my gym membership, which is ironic if I'm training to work in one. Then I'd move somewhere cheaper with my cousin.

say: I'd say we must **move fast** and government needs a **bridge**.
I'd be **practical**, not angry, though tips would feel pointless.
think: I think my **whole job** goes, and the gym side gig too.
The **robot delay** doesn't help, since I don't work with my hands.
do: Get a **coaching qualification** and work as a personal trainer.
Keep running ads **until the last day** and save everything.
feel: Alarmed, like moving because **the building's on fire**.
S2.quote: A robot can count reps, but it can't make you feel guilty for skipping the gym.
fieldNote: He pivots to **personal training**, drawing on his football past.
He sees his side gig vanish too: **gyms use AI themselves**.
His centre view: wants a **government bridge**, framed as practical.

steps.text: Get a football coaching and personal trainer qualification
Apply to work as a personal trainer at a local gym
Save every spare bit until the ad job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now. I'd be helping colleagues figure out their options. I'd still be pro-tools, just realistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I've got about three good years left in ads, then it narrows. Five years means I can build up the trainer side slowly instead of jumping. I'd be thirty-two when it lands, which is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the trainer qualification in evenings this year, then start with a few clients on weekends. I'd keep the ad job and try to get to two months' savings. And I'd keep a couple of gym ad clients until they don't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a good way. Like I've got a plan and the clock is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret leaving behind in marketing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, the numbers. I like seeing what works. Maybe I'd use that with training clients, tracking their progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk you'd mess this up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. Five years feels long, and I could waste two of them. I'd need to set myself deadlines.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough if you start now.
I'd help **colleagues** work out their options, staying realistic.
think: I think I have about **three good years** left in ads.
Five years lets me build the **trainer side** slowly.
do: Do the **trainer qualification** in evenings this year.
Take **weekend clients** while keeping the ad job.
Build up to **two months** of savings.
feel: Anxious, but with **a fair clock** and a plan.
S3.quote: Five years feels long, and I could waste two of them.
fieldNote: He knows his main risk is **getting comfortable**.
He'd carry his love of **numbers** into training clients.
More time turns panic into a **staged switch**.

steps.text: Finish a personal trainer qualification in evenings this year
Train weekend clients while keeping the ad job
Build savings up to two months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time and nobody should be caught out. I'd be telling everyone to use it. I'd also say firms should help pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine in this one. Ten years is a whole career for the ad side, and I'd move up, earn more, and switch when it suits me. I might even run my own small fitness and marketing thing by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in ads three or four more years, get promoted, and save properly for once. Then I'd mix training clients with running AI ads for gyms, until the gyms do it themselves. I'd keep the coaching badge up to date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, honestly. A bit of nerves, but mostly I'd feel lucky with that much time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still be on thin savings for a few years. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. One bad month can still sting. But ten years gives me time to fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind about leaving marketing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I became really good at the budget side. Then maybe I'd stay and run teams of AI tools. I'd go wherever the money and the fun is.

I'd say **firms** should help pay for retraining.
think: I think I'd be **fine** in this one.
I could run my own **fitness and marketing** business by then.
do: Stay in ads **three or four years** and get promoted.
Mix **training clients** with running AI ads for gyms.
feel: Pretty **relaxed**, feeling lucky to have that much time.
S4.quote: I'd go wherever the money and the fun is.
fieldNote: He expects his **income to hold**, so this one barely worries him.
Thin savings still make **one bad month** sting.
He keeps two paths open: **trainer** or AI ad lead.

steps.text: Stay in sports drink ads and aim for promotion
Run AI ads and training sessions for local gyms
Save properly once the pay rise comes

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My job and my side gig both go in the same year, and there's no cushion. What would help is fast, cheap qualifications for hands-on jobs, like coaching, and some income bridge while you get them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how being fast with AI isn't the same as being safe from it. People think because I use AI all day I'm protected, but I'm just closer to the edge so I can see it.

headlineQuote: People think because I use AI all day I'm protected, but I'm just closer to the edge so I can see it.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old** junior ad buyer at a sports drink brand who uses AI daily.
He has **two weeks' savings**, a student loan and shares a flat with his cousin.
He moves fast: **gym side gigs** now, a personal trainer qualification if AGI looms.
He goes from uneasy to **alarmed** under fast AGI, and relaxed with ten years.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, losing his **job and side gig** in the same year.
whatWouldHelp: **Fast, cheap qualifications** for hands-on jobs, plus an income bridge.
